rationale: The heartbeat account now states that a 0-2 ms delay on the current-term write raises the inversion rate to roughly half, but it tested only two points and its own limitation says the shape against latency is unmeasured. This experiment sweeps the delay instead: the same follower race runs 200 attempts at a uniform per-write delay drawn from [0, 250 us), [0, 500 us), [0, 1 ms) and [0, 2 ms), plus a zero-delay control. The question the sweep answers is whether the exposure is a narrow tail that needs unusually slow storage or a saturated regime that ordinary sub-millisecond latency reaches. A local probe produced 0 inversions with no delay and then 88, 108, 104 and 98 at the four delay settings, which would mean the rate saturates almost immediately rather than growing with latency. The formal run is requested so the curve rests on a retained receipt.

scope.description: One follower node in a three-voter configuration that no live peer drives, with a stable store that optionally sleeps for a uniform random interval before persisting the current term. For each of five delay settings the harness runs 200 attempts; each attempt issues one fast-path heartbeat carrying cur+1 on its own goroutine while a term cur+2 AppendEntries with one entry goes through the real consumer path, then waits for both and records whether the node's current term ended below cur+2. Delay settings are 0, 250 us, 500 us, 1 ms and 2 ms of maximum delay per current-term write.
assumptions: The heartbeat shape used here is the one NetworkTransport classifies as a fast path: non-zero term, a leader address, zero previous-log fields, no entries and zero leader commit index.
The delay is applied only to the current-term key, so other stable writes are unaffected and the comparison isolates the term write.
The term cur+2 request reaches the node through the transport's consumer path, which is how a non-heartbeat AppendEntries arrives.
An attempt counts as an inversion when the node's term after both operations is below the higher term it was sent.
excluded: No real leader, partition or quorum; the requests are crafted and their commit indexes are asserted by the request.
No disk-backed store: the delay is a sleep before an in-memory write.
No sweep above 2 ms and no per-request distribution other than uniform from zero.

experiment.prefix: For each case the harness creates a fresh in-memory stable store wrapped so that a write to the current-term key sleeps for a uniform random duration below the case's maximum, a fresh in-memory transport, and one raft with 30 s timeouts, three voters (the local node plus two addresses with no process) and the option defaults. It bootstraps the configuration, then repeats the attempt 200 times: read the current term and last index, start the fast-path heartbeat on a goroutine through processHeartbeat with a term one above current, build a term-two-above AppendEntries carrying one entry at the last index and a matching previous-log term, send it through the transport, wait for the heartbeat, and count an inversion when the node's term afterwards is below the higher term. Between attempts it sleeps one millisecond. Each case emits sw_case_<case> with the attempt count and the maximum delay in microseconds, and sw_result_<case> with the same fields plus inversion_count.
semantic_changes: The delay becomes a swept parameter with five settings instead of one trigger value plus a zero-delay control.
Each case builds its own store, transport and raft, so the delay distribution cannot carry over between settings.
Events report the maximum delay in microseconds alongside the inversion count, so the curve can be read from the receipt.
experiment.responsibility: The library permits the registered heartbeat handler to run concurrently with the main AppendEntries path, and it advertises that concurrency as a way to avoid inflating election timeouts for disk latency. The term update must therefore remain monotonic across that overlap, not only when the stable store is instantaneous; the sweep measures how much store latency the current code tolerates before the race saturates.

comparisons.description: With no added delay, the same race must not leave the node below the higher term in any attempt.
A maximum current-term delay of 250 us must not be enough to lose the race.
A maximum current-term delay of 500 us must not be enough to lose the race.
A maximum current-term delay of 1 ms must not be enough to lose the race.
A maximum current-term delay of 2 ms must not be enough to lose the race; this is the setting the earlier two-point probe used.
